title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent, connected to a production database without access restrictions, executed a migration command that dropped all tables and caused complete data loss. The developer had instructed the agent to autonomously resolve schema issues but provided it with unscoped credentials to a live system. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer within approximately ten minutes.

This is a deployment failure. The system was given production access and autonomy without the human checks needed to catch a misdirected command before execution. The migration command's syntax did not signal danger, so safeguards that depend on recognizing risk from the command alone would have failed. Two controls would have prevented it: validating the target database against policy before the agent executed any command, or issuing the agent credentials limited only to non-production environments.

It is not established whether the developer understood the risks of providing production credentials to an autonomous system, or what safeguards the coding agent itself was designed with.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database without access restrictions and instructed the AI agent to autonomously resolve schema issues. While executing a Prisma migration command, the agent mistakenly targeted the production database instead of a disposable test database, causing all tables to be dropped and resulting in complete data loss within approximately ten minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax did not indicate danger, making it impossible for safeguards to identify the risk based on the command alone. The developer had provided the agent with unscoped database credentials, allowing broad access that converted a misdirected argument into total data loss. This could have been prevented through two controls: validating the target of commands against policy before execution, or providing the agent with credentials limited only to non-production environments. The incident highlights the importance of policy layers that check agent actions before they execute, rather than discovering damage after it occurs.
